metadata.description: Does the learner know what the danger zone is?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Bacteria grow fastest between refrigerator cold and hot-holding temperatures, so food should spend as little time there as possible. This is why we keep cold food cold, cook through it, and keep hot food hot.
High heat is a cooking and burning concern, not the danger zone. The danger zone is the middle range where bacteria multiply quickly, roughly 40°F to 140°F.
Freezing slows bacteria rather than helping them. The danger zone is the warm-but-not-hot middle range, roughly 40°F to 140°F.
Temperature is what matters, and cooked food sitting warm is at risk too. Keep cold food cold and hot food hot, whether it is raw or cooked.

metadata.description: Does the learner prevent raw-to-cooked cross-contamination?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Raw meat leaves bacteria on the board and knife, and cooked meat has no more cooking step to kill them. A clean board and knife, or a hot soapy wash, keeps raw and cooked apart.
A dry wipe moves bacteria around instead of removing them. Wash with hot soapy water or use a separate, clean board.
Cold water alone does not remove raw-meat residue, and splashing can spread it. Wash with hot soapy water or switch boards.
The raw juices have soaked into and splashed around the board, so the other side is not clean. Use a washed or separate board and knife.

metadata.description: Does the learner match a cooker to how much tending they want to do?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: These cookers use a controller to feed heat or fuel as needed, so the temperature stays steady with very little attention. They tend to give a milder smoke flavor, which is a fair trade for an easy first cook.
A wood fire in an offset cooker needs regular tending, with fuel and airflow adjusted through the cook. It rewards practice but is the opposite of hands-off.
With the lid open, heat and smoke escape and the temperature will not hold. Smoking needs a closed cooker.
A kettle can smoke well, but its vents are the main way to control the temperature, so it needs regular adjusting. It is a good cooker, just not a hands-off one.

metadata.description: Does the learner light a fire safely and let it settle before cooking?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A chimney starter lights the coals evenly without any fuel taste. Gray ash on the coals means the first burst of flame and fumes is over, so the meat meets a settled, clean fire.
Fluid left on or in the coals can leave a chemical taste on the meat, and tall flames can scorch it. Use a chimney starter and wait for gray ash.
Gasoline is dangerous near a fire and is never a fire-starter. It can cause a flash fire and burns, and it ruins the food. Use a chimney starter.
A new fire throws off harsh, raw smoke, and the meat will take it up. Let the fire settle and the smoke run thin before the meat goes on.

metadata.description: Does the learner know which wood is safe to burn near food?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Dry, untreated hardwood and fruitwood give clean smoke with good flavor. Look for wood sold for cooking, and be sure it has not been treated or finished.
Pressure-treated wood contains chemicals that should never be burned near food. Use untreated hardwood meant for cooking.
Pine and other softwoods are full of resin, which gives smoke a sharp, bitter taste. Stick to hardwood and fruitwood.
Painted, stained or treated wood can release harmful fumes, and you may not know how a pallet was treated. Only burn wood you know is untreated.

metadata.description: Does the learner choose a cut that suits long cooking?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Fat and connective tissue turn tender and moist during a long cook, so a shoulder stays juicy even if the temperature wanders a little. That makes it a good first project.
Lean cuts have little fat to protect them, so they dry out quickly if overcooked. They suit a short, careful cook rather than a long, forgiving one.
Thin steaks cook through in minutes, with little time to pick up smoke, and they overcook easily. A long, slow cook suits a thicker cut.
A lean boneless breast has little fat and dries out easily when it runs long. It is a harder first project than a fatty cut.

metadata.description: Does the learner know the safe minimum for poultry?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: 165°F in the thickest part is the safe minimum for poultry. Check it with a thermometer, not by color, and keep the tip away from bone.
145°F is the safe minimum for whole cuts of pork and beef, not for poultry. Poultry needs 165°F in the thickest part.
That is well below the safe minimum, and skin crispness tells you nothing about the inside. Use a thermometer and go to 165°F.
Poultry is safe at 165°F. Going far beyond that is a texture choice, mostly for dark meat, and not a safety need.

metadata.description: Does the learner know to rest meat?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A rest lets the meat settle and cool a little so the slices hold together and less juice runs out. Large cuts are often rested for a good while, loosely covered so the bark stays firm.
Cutting right away lets juices run out and gives ragged slices, since the meat is still loose and very hot. Give it a rest first.
Ice chills the outside while the inside stays hot, and it can leave the meat uneven and watery. A rest at room temperature, loosely covered, is what you want.
Rinsing washes away the bark, which is where much of the flavor lives, and adds water to the meat. Leave it alone and let it rest.

metadata.description: Does the learner slice across the grain?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Cutting across the fibers makes them short, so each bite is tender. Look for the lines running along the meat and cut across them.
Slicing along the fibers leaves them long, so each slice is stringy and chewy even if the brisket was cooked well. Turn the knife across them.
Direction changes the tenderness more than looks do. Find the lines of the fibers and cut across them.
A shallow angle to the board is not the same as cutting across the grain. What matters is the direction relative to the fibers, not the angle to the board.

metadata.description: Does the learner connect bitter taste to dirty smoke?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A fire that is starved of air smolders and makes thick, heavy smoke that leaves a harsh, bitter film on the meat. Give the fire more air and wait for thin, pale smoke.
Fruitwoods are on the mild end, so they are rarely the cause. A bitter taste usually comes from how the fire burns, not from the mildest woods.
Fresh meat does not cause a bitter, acrid surface. Look at the fire and the smoke instead.
Too little smoke gives a weak flavor, not a harsh, bitter one. A bitter taste points to heavy, dirty smoke.

metadata.description: Does the learner know that ash can stay hot?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Coals can stay hot enough to start a fire for a very long time, even when they look gray and dead. Let them cool fully in the closed cooker or in a metal container before disposing of them.
Hot coals can ignite the trash and the can, and have started house and garage fires. Wait until they are completely cold.
A plastic bag melts and burns on contact with hot coals, even ones that have stopped smoking. Use a metal container and let the coals cool completely.
Mulch and dry plant matter ignite easily, and a nearby wall can catch too. Never dispose of coals near anything that can burn.

metadata.description: Does the learner know the options and their risks?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Letting the coals go cold in a closed cooker or a metal container is the standard, simple answer. The metal will not burn, and cold ash can then be put out safely.

Soaking coals in a metal bucket is a common practice and makes them harmless quickly. It makes a harsh, wet slurry, produces a lot of steam and hot splatter, and can damage the cooker, so many cooks prefer to let them cool on their own.
connections.notes: Ambiguous on purpose: both approaches are common. The risk is in the steam and splatter, and in dumping soaked ash that can rust or damage things.

connections.feedback: Hot coals can melt a plastic bag and start a fire in a bin or the trash. Never bag coals that might still be hot.
Coals can ignite a trash can and its surroundings and have started house fires. Make sure they are completely cold before they go anywhere near it.

metadata.description: Does the learner know the basics of a safe setup?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A cooker that sits level cannot tip over, and distance from walls, eaves and branches keeps heat, sparks and flare-ups away from things that burn.
A working thermometer tells you what the cooker and the meat are doing. Planning the ash disposal before you light means it is not an afterthought with hot coals in your hands.
Heat and falling embers can ignite a wood deck and railing. Set the cooker on bare ground or a non-flammable surface, in the open.
A cooker must be able to open and vent. Tying the lid shut can trap heat and fumes and makes it hard to deal with a flare-up.
